ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Paediatrics is the medical specialty focused on health care of infants, children and adolescents. It integrates growth, development, disease prevention and treatment tailored to age‑specific physiology.

sections.p: Paediatrics is the branch of medicine dealing with children from birth to 18 years, emphasizing growth, development, and disease management appropriate to each age group.
b: Clinical assessment, growth charts, developmental milestones, vaccination records

sections.p: Severity is judged by impact on growth, development and organ function. Staging uses age‑specific criteria such as WHO growth standards and developmental scales.
b: Growth percentile, developmental delay scores, organ dysfunction grading

sections.p: Common causes vary by age: infections (respiratory, diarrhoeal, vaccine‑preventable), congenital anomalies, nutritional deficiencies, and environmental exposures.
b: Infections (e.g., RSV, rotavirus), malnutrition, congenital heart disease, birth defects, exposure to toxins

sections.p: Presentation depends on age: infants show feeding issues, fever, irritability; toddlers may have failure to thrive; adolescents present with psychosocial or chronic disease symptoms.
b: Fever, poor feeding, failure to thrive, behavioural changes, chronic pain

sections.p: Investigations are guided by clinical suspicion and resource availability.
b: If a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and basic bedside tests such as pulse oximetry, temperature, and physical exam

t.b: Assess anemia, infection, inflammation; low Hb suggests anemia, high WBC suggests infection.
Markers of inflammation; elevated values support bacterial infection.
Detect pneumonia, congenital lung disease; abnormal infiltrate indicates infection.
Identify urinary tract infection or renal disease; leukocytes or nitrites suggest infection.
Evaluate electrolytes, renal function; abnormalities guide fluid and electrolyte management.
Confirm immunisation status; gaps indicate need for catch‑up.

sections.p: Urgent signs include respiratory distress, shock, seizures, severe dehydration, or unexplained bleeding.
b: Respiratory distress, altered consciousness, hypotension, severe pallor, uncontrolled bleeding

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for complications. Drug choice considers age‑specific pharmacokinetics and safety.
b: Avoid high‑dose steroids unless indicated; monitor for side effects

t.b: Choose narrow‑spectrum, age‑appropriate drug; avoid nephrotoxic or ototoxic agents in infants.
Use isotonic crystalloids; monitor for overload in heart disease.
Use acetaminophen; avoid NSAIDs in dehydration or renal impairment.

sections.p: Regular growth monitoring, developmental screening, immunisations, and health education are essential.
b: Growth chart review every visit, developmental milestones check, catch‑up immunisations, nutrition counselling

sections.p: Common misdiagnoses include viral vs. bacterial infections, functional abdominal pain vs. gastroenteritis, and normal developmental variation vs. delay.
b: Functional abdominal pain vs. diarrhoea, viral bronchiolitis vs. bacterial pneumonia, normal speech delay vs. autism spectrum

sections.p: Lab values can be falsely normal in early infection or low in malnutrition; imaging may miss small lesions.
b: CRP may be low in early sepsis, Hb low in iron deficiency may mask infection, chest X‑ray may miss small pneumonias

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress, persistent high fever, seizures, shock, unexplained bleeding, severe dehydration, altered consciousness

faq.q: What is the most common cause of childhood pneumonia?
faq.a: Bacterial infection, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae, is the most common cause.

faq.q: How often should a child be immunised?
faq.a: Vaccinations follow the national schedule, typically starting at birth and continuing through adolescence.

faq.q: When is it safe to give antibiotics to a child?
faq.a: When clinical signs point to bacterial infection, or when a confirmed bacterial pathogen is identified.

exam: Explain the rationale for the WHO growth monitoring chart in paediatric assessment.
Describe the steps to manage a child with suspected sepsis in a low‑resource setting.
Differentiate between viral bronchiolitis and bacterial pneumonia based on clinical features and investigations.
